Pielou's index keeps responding to the rare tail, since a species at 5 percent contributes a twentieth of the sum, while Simpson's index only asks whether two random draws share a species, which the rarest species influences at order 0.0025. questions.explanation: The two lists have identical richness and identical overlap, and a dissimilarity built from those two numbers alone cannot tell them apart. What differs is the process. In one case the community has lost its rarest species and kept the common ones; in the other it has lost a common species and gained a new one that has displaced nothing. The first is a local process, a species going locally extinct from a site, and it is the signature of a driver acting on that site. The second is regional, a species arriving for the first time, and it is the signature of a dispersal route opening, an introduction or a recovery. These call for opposite responses: the first asks what is removing the species, the second asks what is adding it. The standard remedy is to split the dissimilarity into a nestedness part and a turnover part, and the split here is stark: turnover is zero, because no species was lost from the region and replaced. So the whole of the value is nestedness, which is a local process. A is the reading that matters most, because treating this value as turnover would send a manager looking for a colonising species that never arrived. A shared count is not a rescue either: 4 species in common out of 5 is high overlap, and yet the identity of the fifth species is the entire question, and a number cannot answer it.

The 25 birds seen twice, the 20 seen only by the first and the 10 seen only by the second account for a union of 55, and the two counts sum to 80, which is twice 25 plus the 30 seen exactly once. The birds neither observer saw are the remainder, 9, and the total closes: that plus the union is 64. What the method has bought is the gap between the naive average of 40 and the estimate of 64, a difference of 24 birds that one observer working alone would have recorded as absent. The method costs a second person and a discipline about not talking during the count, and the discipline is the harder of the two: 9 birds were seen by neither observer, and nothing in the two counts says what they were.

The exponent is the step people get wrong: this is a count per unit area, so moving to per square kilometre means multiplying by a million, not dividing. The flat-detection assumption is doing all of the work in the division, and it is what fixes the effective half-width at 20 m. If a bird at 19 m is as likely to be seen as one at 1 m, then a 40 m strip is honest, and the same 12 detections over a 30 m strip would have implied 800 birds per square kilometre instead. In detections per 100 m of line the count is 2.4, which is a useful figure because it is independent of the strip width and can be compared between surveys of the same method. Real detection functions fall off with distance, so a real transect reports an effective strip width narrower than the physical one and a correspondingly higher density, which is why the assumption belongs on the record rather than left implicit in the number.

questions.explanation: For a Poisson count the chance of zero is the exponential of minus the mean, so the answer is 4.54e-05, which is 0.00454 percent, or about 45 parts per million. The regularised incomplete gamma function reaches the same quantity by a different numerical route and agrees to fourteen decimal places. The figure is startlingly small, and the reason is that a mean of 10 copies is a long way from zero. A site in serious trouble reaches that condition long before, and at a mean of 1 copy per litre the chance of a zero read is 0.368, which is a different situation entirely. Halving the concentration to 5 copies per litre raises the miss probability to 6.74e-03, still negligible, and the curve is steep enough that the interesting range of a detection assay is the decade below its threshold rather than the decade above it. Two practical points follow. The threshold here is set at the mean, so about half the reads from a true site fall below it and sensitivity is halved without the mean moving at all. And a negative read is worth almost nothing here: three independent tubes all reading zero has probability 9.4e-14, so a single negative cannot be evidence of absence at any concentration a monitoring programme would act on.

questions.explanation: The design effect is 1 plus 3 times 0.30, which is 1.9, and the effective sample size is 16 divided by that, 8.4. The second number is the one that matters, because it is what a precision calculation should rest on and it is not the number that gets written in a methods section. The closed form was verified without using it: 40000 simulated samples of 4 clusters of 4 units drawn with that correlation give a clustered standard error against a simple random one in a ratio of 1.903, which is the design effect measured from the variance rather than predicted from the correlation, and it agrees with 1.9 to three figures. The mechanism is worth stating because the effect is neither subtle nor reduced by working harder inside a cluster. All four units of a cluster share one local condition, so they carry close to one independent piece of information however many are measured, and the standard error grows with the square root of the design effect, 1.378 times larger here, rather than with the design effect itself. To hold a standard error constant, the scattered design needs 16 times 1.9, about 30 units. And a design effect measured from a pilot's own data, rather than assumed, is worth having before the money is spent on the main survey rather than after.

A design effect of 3.72 on only 4 clusters means the effective sample size of those 16 units is about 4.3, so the pilot is a small one reporting a large effect and the estimate of the correlation is itself uncertain. That is the gap. Four clusters give three degrees of freedom for the between-cluster variance, which is why the clustered standard error, 3.18, sits more than twice the value 1.5 that the scattered design achieves, and why neither number should be quoted to two decimal places. The pilot has also not established that the effect is constant across the strata of interest: one correlation measured in one stratum is an assumption everywhere else, and it is the assumption most often carried silently into the main survey. C is the opposite error, reading the two standard errors as measuring the same thing when one comes from 4 clusters and the other from 16 independent units. The pilot's value is in licensing a design, not in fixing a number, and the main survey needs many more clusters than four.

The same answer comes from taking the square root before the ratio rather than after, since twice the observed distance times the square root of the density is twice 130 times 0.005, that is 1.3, and the identity is worth having because it avoids the intermediate distance entirely. An index above 1 means the stems sit further apart than chance would place them, so the pattern is regular or inhibited; below 1 would mean clumped. The number alone does not settle it. With 25 stems that is a real signal, and it is the index together with the randomisation test that carries it.

questions.explanation: The mean of the 16 values, 2.569, is subtracted from each, then I is the number of plots times the weighted cross-product of the deviations, divided by the sum of their squares, with the weights normalised by their total of 16. The sum of squared deviations is 20.55 and the weighted cross-product term is 6.499, so dividing gives I = 0.316. The value has a scale and the scale is not zero to one. Under no spatial pattern the expectation is minus 1 over n minus 1, which for 16 plots is -0.067, so a figure near zero is not evidence of independence, it is the value expected under independence. A reading of 0.316 sits well above that and means neighbouring plots resemble each other more than distant ones do. The second route to the same conclusion uses no formula at all. Shuffling the 16 values among the 16 plots 20000 times and recomputing the statistic each time gives a mean of -0.066 and a standard deviation of 0.116, and none of the 20000 came near 0.316, so the permutation p-value is under 0. The randomised mean of -0.066 sits within 0.001 of the theoretical expectation, which is a second confirmation of the weight construction. A statistic that is unremarkable against its own null distribution and one that is extreme against it are different claims, and this grid is the second kind.

questions.explanation: Semivariance is half the square of the difference, and the differences were chosen so the four classes come out clean. Half of 2.83 squared is 4, half of 5.66 squared is 16, half of 8.49 squared is 36 and half of 8.94 squared is 40. The mean over all 12 pairs is 24, and the same figure comes out without computing the pairs separately, as half the mean of the squared differences, which is the check that the class means are weighted correctly. What the sequence says is a variogram: semivariance rises steeply from 2 to 12 km and then flattens, reaching 36 at 12 km and only 4 more by 30 km. Three parameters are read off a curve like this. The sill is the flat part, 40. The range is the distance at which the sill is reached, about 12 km, and it is the distance beyond which two plots carry no information about one another. The nugget is the semivariance at zero separation, extrapolated from the first class, about 4 against a sill of 40, so a tenth of the sill is 0.1 of variation present at zero distance, which is what measurement error and micro-scale variation look like. What must not be read off a curve is a gradient in the far field: the rise from 36 to 40 is the sill being reached, not a direction in the landscape.

questions.explanation: It tells the interpolator three things and forbids a fourth. The sill is the overall variance of the field, 40, and no amount of sampling reduces the error below it, so a map built from these stations will carry that irreducible spread and it belongs in the uncertainty. The range is about 12 km, and the two end stations 10 km apart are therefore just inside it, which is why a block that size is worth interpolating at all; had the range been 4 km, those two stations would have been independent and the middle station would have been the only thing holding the block together. The nugget is 4, a tenth of the sill, and it is the part of the variance present even between neighbouring plots, so a prediction should never be quoted as more certain than the nugget permits however short the distance. What the variogram forbids is the obvious move, and this is what B gets wrong: the semivariance at 30 km is only 4 above its value at 12 km, which looks like a mild gradient and invites a trend fitted across the block. It is not a gradient. The flattening is the range, and beyond it the field is uncorrelated, so a trend fitted out there is fitting noise. C confuses the sill with the range, treating a variance as a distance limit, and D reads the nugget as the variance of the whole field rather than as the part no distance can explain.

questions.explanation: The three distances come out of the right-angled triangles on the map: 50 km for A, 30 km for B and 40 km for C, each verified by squaring the legs. The inverse-square weights are therefore 1 over 2500, 1 over 900 and 1 over 1600, and the nearest station carries 52 percent of the total weight, which is the intuition the method is built on. Weighting the three readings and dividing by the sum of the weights gives 7.662. The unweighted mean of the same three readings is 7.233, so the interpolation sits 0.428 above it, pulled towards the two higher stations by the weighting. The choice of exponent is a real choice and the result moves with it: weights proportional to the inverse of distance rather than its square give 7.434, which is 0.201 above the mean and 0.228 below the inverse-square estimate. So the answer lies between 7.434 and 7.233 and depends on a convention the method does not state for itself. A reader has to be told which exponent was used. Inverse distance weighting has the merit of being transparent and the defect of being blind: the estimate at any point is pulled towards whichever station is closest, whatever is happening in the field, and a barrier between the two produces a smooth map of a discontinuity.

The share is 4200 over 12000, which is 0.35 or 35 percent, and that part needs no area units at all. The two exponents in this item are the whole of it and both are worth checking by hand. A hectare is 10000 square metres because a hundred metres to the power of two, and a square kilometre is 100 hectares because a kilometre is a thousand metres and area scales with the square, so 1e6 over 1e4 is 100. Getting either wrong puts the answer out by two orders of magnitude, which is exactly the error that turns a 378 hectare class into a plausible-looking number a hundred times larger. In square metres the same area is 3.8 million, and that figure is the one to check against when two reports disagree, because it is the least likely to have been scaled.

What does not follow is that the fine product is right. questions.explanation: The difference is 0.230 and the sum is 0.390, and the ratio is 0.59. The index can be rewritten as one minus twice the red reflectance divided by the sum, which is 1 minus 0.16 over 0.39, or 0.59, and the two routes agreeing is a check that the denominator was the sum and not something else. Two failure modes are worth pricing. Dividing by the sum of the two plus one, which treats a red reflectance of 0.08 as if it were 1, gives 0.176. Scaling the difference by a thousand without dividing gives 230 in per mille, which is a real number in a real unit and is not the index. The index lies between minus one and plus one by construction and lands near zero on bare soil where the two bands read alike, which is what makes it a vegetation index rather than a reflectance. The gain over a single-band measurement is that it partly cancels the illumination, since scaling both reflectances by the same factor leaves the ratio unchanged. The limitation is saturation: a dense canopy with a red reflectance of 0.040 and a near-infrared reflectance of 0.480 gives 0.846, and doubling the leaf cover again moves the index very little, so the index cannot distinguish a moderately closed canopy from a completely closed one. On bare soil of red 0.100 and near-infrared 0.420 the same index would be 0.615, which is the point of the soil-adjusted variant in a later item.

questions.explanation: Multiplying the three factors gives 1698.5 grams of carbon per square metre per year. The conversion to a hectare is the step to check: one hectare is 10000 square metres and one kilogram is 1000 grams, so a figure in grams per square metre is multiplied by 10 to reach kilograms per hectare, giving 16985 kilograms of carbon per hectare per year. The same production expressed per square kilometre is 1698 tonnes of carbon per square kilometre per year, and the factor between those two numbers is exactly 10, which is worth checking by hand rather than assuming. A hectare is a hundredth of a square kilometre and a tonne is a thousand kilograms, so a hectare holds one hundredth as much per unit area as a square kilometre and a tonne is a thousand times a kilogram: the two factors are a hundredth and a thousand, and they multiply to ten, so the per-hectare figure is ten times the per-square-kilometre figure, 16985 against 1698. Getting that factor wrong in either direction is a power of ten, and it is the single most common error in a regional carbon budget. The result rests on two assumptions the arithmetic cannot test. The light use efficiency of 1.2 grams per megajoule is a stand-in for a real leaf, and it varies with species, season and water supply. The radiation figure is a total for the year, and a pixel with the same index and half the radiation fixes half the carbon, so the product is 510 grams of carbon per square metre per year in the same year with 30 percent of the radiation. A model of this kind is a good map of relative differences between pixels and a poor absolute budget, and that distinction is the one to keep whenever a figure like this is quoted.

questions.explanation: Taking logarithms of the attenuation equation gives the leaf area index as minus the natural logarithm of the transmitted fraction divided by the coefficient, which is minus ln 0.30 over 0.50, or 2.408. Putting that back through the exponential returns 0.3, which is the fraction of light that was measured, and that round trip is the check worth making every time, because a sign error in the logarithm is the usual way this goes wrong and it produces a negative index that is visibly impossible. Half the light, for comparison, corresponds to an index of 1.39. The number is a ratio of areas, leaf surface to ground surface, so it is written in square metres per square metre and can exceed one with no difficulty: an index of 3 means three square metres of leaf for every square metre of ground, stacked or horizontal, and values of 4 to 6 in a closed tropical canopy are ordinary. Two things the index does not settle. It says nothing about the vertical distribution of the foliage, so a stand with all its leaves in a single thin layer can have the same index as one distributed through several metres and behave quite differently for a seedling underneath. And it depends on the coefficient, which is a property of canopy geometry and sun angle, so an index computed at a low sun angle will exceed one computed at noon on the same canopy.

What the total rests on is the part that matters, because this is a modelled number being reported as a quantity. The per-square-metre figure is the product of an index, a radiation total and a light use efficiency, and the last of those is a stand-in whose value depends on species, season and whether the water was there. Extending one cell's figure to 1250 square kilometres multiplies every one of those assumptions by that factor, and the uncertainty in the total is at least as large as the uncertainty in the input, never smaller. answer.ex: The design has to face two separate problems, and a longer series or a larger sample solves neither. The first is the missing control: with every site inside the area of interest, there is no way to separate a change caused by whatever is being studied from a change caused by something that hit the whole region, and a third year of falling counts will not supply the comparison. The remedy is to start recording a set of matched reference sites now, outside the influence of the cause, on the same habitat, soil and aspect, and to report the difference in the change between the two sets. That is weak evidence for the earlier years because the reference series has no history, and it has to be said so rather than quietly back-fitted. A stronger remedy is archaeological in the useful sense: gather the survey's own herbarium and photographic records for the earlier years, which are independent of the counts and were collected before anyone knew what they would show. The second problem is the measure. A count of flowering plants is not a count of plants, and flowering varies with the weather in the year, so the same population can produce a 40 percent swing in a bad spring. The survey must record a measure of plant condition or a second count in a fixed window, and it must report flowering phenology alongside the count, so that a bad year is visible as a bad year. Three further points. The three pairs of sites that sit in the driest hollows need their own stratum, because a fall concentrated there and a fall spread evenly imply different processes. One of the twenty fell 90 percent in a single year, and a single site cannot distinguish a species collapsing from a quadrat being lost to bramble, so the survey needs permanent markers and a recorded reason for any site that is lost. And the analysis belongs on the difference in changes between the two sets, with the year as a repeated measure on each site, because sites within a set are not independent of one another and treating forty counts as forty independent observations would shrink the standard error by roughly the square root of twenty. Eight years of one series is worth having, and it is not worth very much without the comparison that eight years cannot supply.

answer.ex: The comparison has to answer a trajectory question, not a level question, and the two need different designs. A level comparison between 11 species and 34 species, that is 32 percent of the reference, is close to meaningless here, because a marsh 3 years out of farming is not supposed to resemble a marsh that was never farmed, and reporting the gap as a failure measures elapsed time rather than recovery. What the design needs is a trajectory, which means the restored marsh has to be resurveyed, and the reference marsh has to be resurveyed in the same years by the same method, so that the two trajectories can be compared as trajectories. Three years is not enough points to fit anything, and the honest design commits to a decade rather than reporting what three years happened to show. The reference should be more than one marsh: a single reference is one sample of what a reference marsh is, and a difference between the two is indistinguishable from a difference between the two sites. Three or four references, matched on hydroperiod, soil and vegetation zone, and analysed with the site as the unit rather than the species, will support a claim; one will not. Detection has to be handled explicitly, because three years after re-wetting a marsh is a place with standing water in some places and none in others, and a plant list is partly a list of what was findable on the day. Repeat visits timed across the season, and a record of the water level, are both required. Two components of the answer deserve particular weight. The species that the restored marsh already has are the informative ones, because a wetland that has lost its rarest species may take decades to lose them and that is a different problem from one that has never acquired the common ones; so the comparison needs a full species list and not a presence and absence summary. And absence of a species in a recovering marsh is close to uninformative, because the propagules have not arrived, whereas presence is informative. Presence and absence therefore need separate treatment in the analysis, and a symmetric index built over them will misreport the trajectory. A second reference question, which the design must also settle, is whether the restored marsh is a marsh at all: its hydrology, and the depth and duration of inundation, are the mechanism the recovery depends on, and a site restored to the wrong water regime will have a species list that no amount of survey will improve.

answer.ex: The question is a movement question, and a movement question has a control and a scale, neither of which a camera or a trap array supplies on its own. Movement through a corridor has to be measured as a difference from movement through similar ground that is not a corridor, so the design needs a set of control sites: woodland strips of the same width in the same landscape that are not planted connectors. Comparing detections in the strip against detections in the controls, at the same effort and with the same gear, is what separates corridor use from corridor construction. The detection method has to be able to register a passage rather than a presence, which means a camera or track pad that records direction or an identifiable animal, not a trap that records an occupancy. Track pads deposited on a fixed grid across the strip and across the controls, with the same spacing in both, do that and are cheap; cameras give identity, which is what tells you whether the animals crossing are the ones that were there before. Two things have to be measured or the result is uninterpretable. The width matters: a 60 m strip is narrow for a large mammal and generous for a small one, so the test has to be run per taxon, and a corridor can work for the taxon it was designed for and be used by nothing else. And the distance matters: use through the strip has to be compared with use along its edges, because an animal walking the margin is not what the corridor was built to enable, and a strip whose use is entirely marginal has not solved the isolation. The two blocks either side also have to be sampled, because corridor use is only interesting where it changes the prospects of a population at one end, and that requires knowing which individuals are in each block, which is a mark and recapture or a genetics question rather than a camera question. A single season of data is not enough, because animal movement is seasonal and a corridor used only in one season is a corridor for one season. Finally, a before and after is not available here, since the strip is already planted, which means the design has to lean on the control sites and on the internal gradient across the strip, and that limitation should be stated in the report rather than glossed by implying a baseline that was never measured.

answer.ex: The correction buys the difference between an observation and a population, and the size of the difference is large: the naive figure of 0.6 understates the occupancy by 24 percent, which corresponds to about 10.5 sites that were occupied and never recorded. That matters operationally, not just arithmetically, because a site recorded as unoccupied is either written off or resurveyed next year, and both responses are wrong for it. The cost is that the correction is only as good as the detection probability behind it, and here that probability was assumed at 0.3 per visit rather than measured, which means the corrected value carries the uncertainty of the assumption on top of the uncertainty of the count. Assuming a per-visit probability of 0.20 instead would give a four-visit probability of 0.59 and an occupancy of 1.016 rather than 0.79, so a small change in an unmeasured assumption moves the answer by several points. There is a second cost, which is the one that makes people distrust the method. The corrected occupancy is a model output, not a count, and a report that quotes it to two decimal places invites a reader to treat it as an observation. Its honest form is a distribution, and a survey that measures the detection probability by repeat visits or by a known-placement test can report one, whereas a survey that assumes it can only report a point. The assumption that does the damage is independence: four visits at a site are treated as independent, and in practice they are not, because a plant is easier to find in flower, so visits clustered into a flowering window miss more often than the arithmetic allows and the true occupancy is lower than the correction reports. Two things make the result usable rather than merely correct. The correction is bounded: it can never return more than 1, and at 0.79 it does not. And it is a statement about the frame that was surveyed, so the frame has to be a probability sample of the landscape rather than a set of convenient sites, because a correction applied to a non-random sample fixes the detection problem and leaves the selection problem untouched.

A mean of 675 hectares is an honest statement about a hypothetical patch, and the median of 107.5 is an honest statement about a typical one, and the fact that the mean is nearly six times the median is an honest statement about how unevenly the habitat is held. The Gini coefficient of 0.746 puts the same imbalance in a single number. Together they answer questions about connectivity, about the area a reserve buys per unit of boundary, and about how much clearing a given number of permitted roads would fragment, and on those questions they are the right summary. They stop being a fair description when a requirement is a threshold rather than an average. A species needing a contiguous core of a thousand hectares is satisfied by 2 of the 12 patches and by none of the others, and no mean is a statement about that. A mean is also a poor description of exposure, because the patch holding 51.9 percent of the habitat carries that share of every risk and that share of every chance of recolonisation. Three further limits are worth naming. These figures know nothing about quality, so two patches of the same area with different vegetation are one number. They know nothing about the corridors between patches, so a landscape of small patches joined by continuous habitat and one of small isolated patches receive the same summary despite behaving nothing alike. And they are a snapshot, so a landscape whose patch count is rising can have a perfectly stable mean and a steadily worsening prospect. The honest way to use a summary like this is to publish it beside its own distribution and beside the requirement it has to meet, and to state whether the summary or the distribution is doing the work in each claim built on it.

answer.ex: An area under a curve and a probability answer different questions, and the confusion between them is the commonest misreading of a suitability map. The area under the curve answers a ranking question: put a presence site and an absence site at random and score both, and the chance that the presence scores higher is 0.649. That is a statement about the whole test set at once, and it says nothing about any individual cell. Converting it into a probability of presence requires a base rate and a choice of threshold, and neither is in the number. The base rate is decisive. Take a cell scoring well, with a sensitivity of 58.3 percent and a false positive rate of 33.3 percent at the cut in use. If the species is at half the sites, then among 24 cells with those scores, 7 are real and 12 are not, and the rule calls 11, so about 64 percent of the cells it calls are real. If the species is instead at one site in a thousand, then a thousand cells with those scores contain 0 real and 24 not, and the rule calls about 4, so about 0 percent of the cells it calls are real. The same curve, the same scores and the same cut, and a factor of twenty between the two answers. A probability of presence is a property of a cell together with a base rate and a rule, and quoting it as a property of the cell alone drops both. A second reason is that the model was fitted on one set of sites, and its scores on any other ground carry an uncertainty that the curve does not report at all: the area under the curve is an average over a sample, and two models with the same curve can differ considerably in their scores at the extremes, which is exactly where a threshold is applied. The honest forms are a predicted probability with its interval and its base rate stated, or a binary map with the threshold published and the error rates beside it. A map that offers neither leaves the reader to supply the one number that cannot be recovered from the model.
